utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Aleksandar Vujic. Mr. Cunningham will be gone maybe all or part of today, back with us tomorrow. May I report very briefly on the treasury department issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I spoke late last night, which was in the afternoon in Washington DC, with a representative from the office of foreign assets control explaining our concern. He agreed that the authorisation that was sent to Judge Meron is not a licence and that the regulations require that we be licensed. His view was that even though it wasn't a licence, it was probably a good Defence in case we are charged with a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wish you luck, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I told him that gave me a lot of comfort. He said what they are doing is they are trying to decide whether to issue individual licences or a group licence, and that they would try to have an answer to that today. I expressed to him that I felt that it was important that they make that decision rather quickly because I didn't like the jeopardy that I was in and so that's where we are and I have advised all members of our association of that situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. And as I did yesterday, I would like you, Madam Registrar, to extract this part from today's transcript and have it communicated to His Excellency, President Meron.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been keeping President Meron well advised as to what I'm doing in this regard so he's getting all my letters and I'm sending sort of daily e-mails to his chef de cabinet so he knows where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I prefer to do it myself, too. President Meron is not someone who sleeps on things. He will act and he will act fast. Thank you. So, Ms. Korner, before you bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I apologise first for two things? The schedule is catching up with me as well. I was unable to list -- to have time to list the documents I was going to use after I'd spoken to the witness so I just said both volumes. I'm not going through both volumes of documents, but I will be going through a number with the witness, particularly in relation to the military operations because he can deal with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I apologise also for the late arrival of proofing notes. They were sent to me by an intern who worked until half past 11.00 at night to get them into some sort of order. For which I'm very grateful. But I'm sorry they arrived so late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't read them as yet but I will go through them as we go along. All right I thank you, Ms. Korner. Yesterday you raised the matter of the exhibit binders for Bosanska Krupa, Celinac and Kotor Varos. Well, I checked with my staff and indeed, none of these binders or none of the binders for these three municipalities have been admitted as yet. The -- yesterday, I made a mistake myself in referring to the documents relating to the Celinac municipality, saying that I remember that there was an objection on the part of Mr. Ackerman. Indeed there was an objection on the part of Mr. Ackerman. The only thing being is that we had discussed that objection here in an open session and I had taken a decision. However, contrary to what you said, Mr. Ackerman, we are all making mistakes now. There does not, at least we tried to go through all the recent documents, which I brought with me too but there doesn't seem to be a Defence response objecting to the exhibits from the Bosanska Krupa municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Your Honour, and I'll try to get to that as quickly as I can, hopefully even today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, because I wouldn't like, since I'm tightening up the belt myself I wouldn't like to put the Prosecution into further restrictions. That having been said, there will be some decisions later on this morning, one will be on Rule 92 bis and also some on protective measures. So expect them later on in the day, probably after the first break because I still have to tie up with two of my staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, on that note may I raise something and I think it's worth raising in open court so Your Honours hear it and Mr. Ackerman. Statements were taken from a number of women who were raped in the Kotor Varos sawmill. We cannot persuade a single one of them to come and testify. The one who was due to testify, who I think is on Your Honour's list near the end, is -- she just had a baby, another small baby, she is psychologically, we are told, incapable of giving evidence. It's the same for all of them. It's perhaps not surprising. Now, Your Honour, we can get, we hope, a Rule 92 bis declaration from at least -- we have already got one from one of them who was put in as Rule 92. We tried to persuade her to testify and the answer is the same there. We are going to ask that Mr. Ackerman be kind enough to accept none of these statements are direct evidence against Mr. Brdjanin, for obvious reasons we couldn't even begin to try and put them in as Rule 92. We would ask that we may be permitted to submit two statements under Rule 92 rather than calling any of these women to relive these experiences. Your Honour, I'm raising it now, I don't expect an answer straight away but so far Mr. Ackerman has not in fact when there have been rape victims insisted that they go through that evidence. And so it may be that that's acceptable but I raise that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest, Ms. Korner, now that you have given fair advance warning to Mr. Ackerman, that you try and file the motion today or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You'd like it in writing would you? We are really drowning with work, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But at least you need to hand in a copy of these statements and an indication of who we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That we won't do in open session obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But no, I'm pretty easy on that. I can live with an oral motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I can hand down an oral decision that's no problem with me but obviously he needs to know who we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman has the statements in any event but we will give him the names and we will hand in the statements to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We can move in that direction if Mr. Ackerman cooperates, and I use cooperate not in the sense that if he says no it means that he's not cooperating. So I want to make myself Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The other matter Your Honour is this, while we are on the subject of documents. We haven't had the decision yet in the journalist witness aspect and I am just wondering whether -- have Your Honours admitted the article? I think Your Honours did say that but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The decision hasn't been handed down for more or less administrative reasons more than anything else. We are still waiting for a document which hasn't arrived as yet. None of us is to blame for that but I wouldn't like to go into details but the position is, yes, the document itself is being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, we will arrange to give it an exhibit number at some stage and hand in a copy properly. Your Honour, then finally, unless Your Honour has any other matters, this witness was granted protective measures but when I spoke to him yesterday, he appeared to be content to testify in open session. I just think it perhaps preferable that Your Honour checks that with him before we do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will but we need -- yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to the first issue that was raised by Ms. Korner, I can just say as a general proposition that in every such instance, we have basically agreed to the testimony regarding the actual sexual assaults themselves. My only concern would be the peripheral matters that might be contained in those statements. But otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to say much more than what I have said until I have seen the statements or someone from my staff has seen those statements. I think we can safely anticipate that if there is anything beyond the sexual crimes, then this will be given due consideration and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, obviously there is the background of how they ever got to the sawmill in the first place so the women do describe the attacks on the villages, what happened to them and how they arrived at the sawmill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may well be -- well, Your Honour, I think the best thing is for Mr. Ackerman to have a look at them and to see whether he can agree them or if he wishes to have excisions or redactions to let us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think we can take it up from there. It was the whole idea, the purpose behind your request is to have some evidence on rapes and basically that. I mean, I don't think you're going to rely on these witnesses to prove that there was an attack on the town or on the village. I don't know but.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think one witness because we thought it would cover both aspects of it but it may be Your Honour we can look at it from a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You make your own assessment and then we will decide accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can promise you our cooperation there. So let's bring down the curtains for the time being until we bring the witness in. Then we will discuss with the witness whether he cares for the protective measures that have already been given, granted to him, and if not, we will go into complete open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I propose to adopt the same system in that I'm going to ask to hand in his statements just in case I'm unable to complete my examination-in-chief properly in the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, unless in fact she is able to -- she is unable to complete her direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll leave it to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She's been given a whole day, I think that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll leave it to the end. At the end of today's sitting we will take the matter up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to give evidence in this trial that has been instituted against Radoslav Brdjanin, and before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Usher, who is standing to your left will be handing you the text of this declaration which I kindly ask you to read out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start from something that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour maybe we better go into, just for moment, private session while you deal with those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now that we are in open session, I can confirm that the witness has chosen out of his own free will to waive the two protective measures that the Chamber had granted him upon specific request by the Prosecution, namely the use of a pseudonym and facial distortion. Now, have you ever given evidence before in your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will just explain very briefly what's going to happen. You know Ms. Korner. Ms. Korner is the lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case. She will be putting to you a series of questions which you need to answer in conformity with the oath that you have taken a few minutes ago. It is anticipated that she will finish her questioning today. Then you will be cross-examined, in other words questioned, by the lead counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin, the lead Defence counsel. That will be tomorrow. Tomorrow I will remind you once more but Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what is important for you to remember is that both Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman have a right to question you. It's not just the Prosecution that has a right to put questions to you but also the Defence, which basically means that you have a corresponding duty, obligation, to answer every question that is put to you irrespective of where it's coming from, irrespective of who is putting the question to you. My last word of advice to you, if you want to return home after tomorrow, is to be brief in your answers and you just answer yes or no when the question requires just that simple answer, and go into details only in as far as you are asked, not beyond what you are asked, all right? Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good luck, Mr. Sadikovic. I leave you in the hands of Ms. Korner, which is not a threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hope Your Honour didn't mean it in the way it sounded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sadikovic, is your name Muhamed Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you born on the 26th of June, 1961?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it's your birthday tomorrow, the day after?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman will help you celebrate it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it right that you are a Bosniak by ethnicity? Nationality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sadikovic, I want to ask you a little bit about your background and then we will go immediately to the events in 1991 and 1992. I think, although born elsewhere, you were actually brought up in the municipality of Kotor Varos, in the actual town itself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you study construction engineering at the university of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Graduating in 1987?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also by that stage, having done your military -- compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then did you return to Kotor Varos where you were employed by a construction company?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thereafter, did you start your own company, manufacturing concrete blocks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this? In the course of your time in the construction industry, did you ever come across Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, did you run this company until the start of the war in Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was on the ground in Istria and Rovinj [phoen] away on business.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you join the SDA in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you a member of the executive board of the party in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the president of the SDA Fikret Djikic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it may be we'll need to go through some of the other members in a moment. Was the deputy president Ahmet Cirkic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the secretary Bakir Dizdar?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there also in Kotor Varos a branch of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: There was, yes, municipal board.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that headed by a gentleman named Anto Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was there also obviously a branch of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who was the president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Nedjeljko Djekanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know both Mr. Djekanovic and Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Mandic was my neighbour, and I knew him much better than Djekanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you this? Did the three political parties operate from the same building within Kotor Varos or were they in separate buildings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: In the early days, they were in different buildings but at a later stage we were all given offices in one and the same building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you roughly tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you I joined them later, after I returned from the field in Croatia, but I think that in late 1991 or perhaps early 1992, they already had premises in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you were -- you worked in the construction industry. However, did there come a time when you entered into employment with the Kotor Varos police force?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. My party fellows decided that I should -- that I could do it because they knew my family, they knew how I was brought up, how I was educated. They knew that I had lived in a city, and that my views were normal and that I would be up to the task.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In order to do that, did you have to have any kind of training?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo at the republican MUP for Bosnia-Herzegovina and I also underwent a short -- I mean for the training, and then I also passed the medical checkup and a test.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Kotor Varos, I think we've heard, was a municipality that had the majority but not an overall majority were Serb, some 14.000 or so. The next biggest proportion being the Muslims, with 11.000 odd and then the Croats with 10.000 odd. How was that ethnic makeup reflected in the police force?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, before the elections, the ethnic structure of the police force was tipped in favour of the Serb population and it was only after the elections that the Croats and Bosniaks put that ethnic structure right so that it was better then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. So roughly -- before you say the elections, it was what, largely a Serb police force? After the elections, there was more of a balance, was there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed. Before the war, attention was not paid to the ethnic structure, that is the ethnic structure of the population was not reflected there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So if you were asked to estimate, when you went into the police, what the structure was percentage wise, what percentage when you went in after the elections were the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly 40 to 45 per cent were Serbs, and the Bosniaks and Croats accounted for some 55 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, we've heard a lot of evidence about how the appointments of police officers, police leaders, the chief and the commander were political appointments, you've told us that your party decided you were the candidate that should be put forward. Was your candidacy accepted without opposition?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: No, my candidacy was not accepted and it took a lot of time for me to get to the police station to work. The Serb representative, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. chief, was appointed immediately, and his superior, and that was Nedjeljko Maric, was appointed by a decision of the republican MUP in September 1991 and I made it finally to the police station in early 1992. I think it was January, because there was a lot of opposition to my joining the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Who was the chief -- who was the Serb representative to the chief, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Savo Tepic was the chief, and the commander was Nedjeljko Maric, representing the Croat population, of course, and I was the third one, deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, who was leading the opposition to your appointment and why?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Head of the public security centre in Banja Luka, that is the whole region, Stojan Zupljanin, and also the head of my office, Savo Tepic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And why were they opposing you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin told me something like he'd heard that I was not a bad man but that he had already a Muslim in the police, Sejdo Tatar, who was a good policeman, a highly competent one, and that as long as he was there, there was no way I could make my way into the police station. And the reason for it was that this gentleman, Sejdo Tatar, was married to a Serb and he thought that he'd be able to manipulate him and that he would do whatever he ordered him to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What rank did Mr. Tatar told in the Kotor Varos police?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that at that time he was a criminal investigation -- that is an inspector in the criminal investigations department in the Kotor Varos station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when did you meet Mr. Zupljanin, when you had this conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: It was when I went to Sarajevo to collect the decision signed by the then minister, and the decision was sent through official channels, like all the other documents, but it was never delivered to me, and I was never invited to come and start performing my duties, but I knew that a decision had been signed so I went to Sarajevo, collected the document, and then went to Mr. Zupljanin to ask him why was it that I could not enter the police station and perform the duties to which I had been assigned. Normally, like my chief and the commander, there was the same procedure, so why couldn't I assume my duties like the other two candidates? I enjoyed the support of the head of the municipality, Anto Mandic, and of course I had the support of the president of my party, and his other associates, and that is why I was issued this decision in Sarajevo and then we all fought together so that I could get into the police station and start performing my duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What I was actually after, it's my fault, Mr. Sadikovic, is roughly what date was this, that you spoke to Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was sometime in October, I think we talked in October, in mid-October.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And you saw him in Sarajevo, is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. In his office in Banja Luka, that is where we met.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you very quickly, please, to look at a document that dealt with your actual appointment, please, Exhibit P2129. Which is after divider -- my bundle, 12. It's dated the 31st of January, 1992. This is an extract from the minutes of the HDZ Kotor Varos municipal board dated the 31st of January, and do we see under item 2, that the president, Anto Mandic, submitted a report on the interparty meeting, the major problem for the continuation of the work of the assembly was the appointment of yourself as the deputy commander of the police, agreement was reached and you started work on the Monday? So as you remember, you started work in January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This proves it. That is I gave you the month. I didn't give you the date. And I have to explain that an inspector from the Sarajevo Ministry of the Interior had to come before I could enter the police station in Kotor Varos and assume my duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, sir, you can put that document away. You took up your position, did you, as the deputy commander of the police station in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in order for you, for the police in Kotor Varos to communicate with the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, could you go directly to them or did you have to go via Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: No. On the chain of command our communication is such that you first report to the chief, to the head of the public security centre in Banja Luka and then they communicate with others, and also, when something comes from Sarajevo, it first goes to Banja Luka and then reaches us in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And were you having any problems with your communication with Sarajevo during the period between January and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, in the early days, there were -- it wasn't difficult, but after the parallel police was formed for the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, communication with Sarajevo was interrupted, it was discontinued and we stopped receiving dispatches and all the rest that we had to receive from Sarajevo. It went to Banja Luka, to the new police, or the -- of Republika Srpska and Kotor Varos was an integral part of that police, without our knowledge or our consent, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Are we talking about after March of 1992, when the -- there was a split in the Ministry of the Interior and the Serbian Ministry of the Interior was set up?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to look at some of the early events in 1992 in Kotor Varos. Could you be shown now, please, P29? Now, this is a decision that apparently was taken by what is described as the Assembly of the Serbian People of Kotor Varos to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and it's dated the 7th of February of 1992. Now, what was the Serbian assembly, as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you that is the highest authority in the Serb region of Bosanska Krajina, that is Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It talks about here, though, in February, 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian People of Kotor Varos. Were you aware of such an assembly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was done unlawfully and in parallel with the parliament, with the assembly which was elected lawfully in the elections of 1991, and that assembly functioned normally after the elections in 1990, and this was a parallel body set up without our knowledge or the -- or the Croatian -- or the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you aware, at the time, in other words in February of 1992, that this so-called assembly had made a decision to join the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't think anybody was wise to it. I certainly wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can give that one back to the usher. In this period of time, that is around February and March of 1992, were you able to receive television broadcasts from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, we couldn't, and that was one of the things that were done in the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, we could not watch Sarajevo television because the relays, the transmitting stations on Vlasic and Kozara were all pointed at Banja Luka and Belgrade so that we could not watch that programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, what were the programmes like that you were receiving from Banja Luka or other areas?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, these were nothing but propaganda programmes which talked about the sufferings, the trials and tribulations of the Serb people throughout its -- their history. The opening of graves where allegedly the Serb people were buried. And such programmes, which suited only one of the peoples, whereas the other two peoples were just ignored, and all these programmes were sending a message that those two peoples were a threat to the Serbs, and that throughout their history the Serbs Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had been under threat and that they had been victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you, during the period between January and June of 1992, ever see Radoslav Brdjanin on television?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the media and the written press and on television and radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know what position he held within the political structures in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew that he was also a member of parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you remember specifically any of the things that he said on television?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: He said that -- that Serb people needed it and that the Serb people had to do it and that the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina would be established and that it would be an integral part of Republika Srpska and that all Serbs had to live in one state. That was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, had the non-Serbs in Kotor Varos responded to the mobilisation following the outbreak of the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, 95 to 98 per cent of Bosniaks and Croats did not respond to the mobilisation. A, they did not want to go to war, and B, they above all didn't want to go to a war in another state and be involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, how did that failure to respond to the mobilisation, by the non-Serbs, affect relationships in the municipality, in the town in particular?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it was also a way to eliminate Muslims, Bosniaks and Croats from the Territorial Defence, because they knew that when the summons came to a Bosniak or a Croat to go to the front in Croatia, that he would refuse to do it, and thereby he would be eliminated from the Territorial Defence, his weapon taken away, and given to -- that is either left in the depots, either stored or given to a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Within Kotor Varos, was the town divided into areas which were specifically Serb, Muslim or Croat, or was it all mixed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it was mixed by and large. Across Bosnia it was mixed, you can't really separate Bosniak or Croat or Serb part because if you have a purely ethnic village somewhere, right next to it is a village with somebody else so that it is impossible to separate, to take out, some territories or parts of territories and have them really ethnically pure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that the failure to respond meant that Muslims didn't have weapons and so on. Was there any other consequence that resulted from the failure to respond to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, under the then law of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was -- that was tantamount to desertion but we didn't understand it like that. We thought that it was a highly moral act because we did not want to go to war and we did not want to attack other peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were the people who failed to respond to mobilisation able to keep their jobs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Until the aggression -- before the aggression, yes, but when power was taken over in Kotor Varos on the 11th of June, Bosniaks and Croats were removed from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you very shortly about arms. During this period, were you aware of Serbs receiving arms, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: I was aware of that, yes. Serbs were armed on three different occasions, weapons were being given to them. A large amount of weapons from Croatia and Slovenia was being transferred into Bosnia. The weapons belonging to the JNA, which had been paid for by all the different peoples of the former Yugoslavia, went to the Serbs, and the officers of the JNA had those weapons put away. Later given only to one of the ethnic armies, which was the case in Kotor Varos and across the other towns too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you say three -- you told us three different occasions.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Three times. The weapons were being handed out three times. Chronologically speaking in January, I believe, February and March, roughly speaking. I'm talking about three different periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you, in the Kotor Varos police station, have weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Being a police station, we did have certain weapons. Each of those working there had a certain amount of weapons, and the reserve police force had been 100 per cent mobilised so we did have our own warehouse containing our own weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, what sort of weapons were they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly automatic and semi-automatic weapons, hand-held launchers, M-53 and short barrel guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to the weapons that were in the Kotor Varos police station?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Just in order to avoid confusion there, we had our own weapons at the police station but in the same building, we had the TO, Territorial Defence warehouse, the weapons from the whole municipality, which had been paid for in peace time by the companies working in the area, certain money, amount of money was put aside to pay for the weapons that were to be used by all the three different ethnic groups. The warehouse was in the same building that our police station was. The policy of the Serbian people, in that period, was clearly indicating that they were preparing for war, so the weapons that were meant for all the three peoples of the municipality had been taken from the warehouse in Kotor Varos to Banja Luka without the consent or without any kind of agreement with the remaining two ethnic groups. All the documents that every municipality had, military administration, with records of military conscripts, military service, the assignments given to conscripts, once their military service had been served, all these documents was in an unfair way whisked away to Banja Luka, as well as all the weapons to keep Muslims and Croats from laying their hands on those weapons and using them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to ask you to look at a document and then ask you about some detail of that. Could you have a look, please, at P2141? Now, Mr. Sadikovic, this is an except from the minutes of the National Defence council dated the 7th of April, and it appears you were present at that meeting. Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because one of the things, if we look at item 1, we see that Lieutenant Colonel Peulic, the commander of the unit based in Kotor Varos, was talking --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Peulic, Peulic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Peulic. Was talking about the locations of the JNA units and then there was a discussion about the Territorial Defence, in which the taking of weapons from the TO depot to Banja Luka, the self-organising of citizens and setting up of units in local communes was discussed and Mr. Tepic, the commander of the TO stressed that weapons had been taken away and put in the Mali Logor barracks in Banja Luka. And then if you -- if we go to the end of the item, we see that there was a discussion about the reserve police force being strengthened, reserve police force should maintain watches in order to avoid the creation of other units and self-organising in villages, and then there was an arrangement for a meeting with Stojan Zupljanin, with representatives from the municipality effectively I think from all three parties. Now I want to take each area in turn. First of all, the removal of the weapons to Banja Luka, had that happened shortly before this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the Serbian policy throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Vlasic and the rest, the communications, they did that and we only discussed later on, but once everything had already been done, and the weapons had already been taken away, and then there was discussion but they had already taken all the documents away. And it was only then that they were prepared to talk. They had their own agenda. Once they had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. carried it out there was a discussion which was no use to us, what could we have done at that point?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Had you been on duty the night that the weapons were taken?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was on duty. I was the officer on duty at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: And about midnight, or just after midnight, 1.00 a.m. perhaps, I can't remember the exact time, inspector Savo Todorovic arrived from Banja Luka and told me to come with him to inspect the local branch stations in Maslovare and Siprage. So I went with him to Maslovare and Siprage to inspect the stations that had been set up there. We didn't reach Siprage because there were problems with the road. There was a bridge there that had been damaged by water. We went to the checkpoints to the station in Maslovare and after that, we went to a cafe to have a drink. However, once I returned, my duty officer, Anto Kljajic told me, boss, while you were away, the weapons were loaded on to trucks from the depot, from the TO depot, army members came and took the weapons to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the other matters that were discussed was that there should be the strengthening of reserve police forces to maintain watches in all local communes in order to avoid the creation of other units and self-organising in the villages. Now, what was actually happening at this stage? Were patrols being set up or barricades?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who were they being set up by?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Kotor Varos had already been blocked, a lot earlier, before the takeover on the 11th of June, it was blocked by checkpoints set up by Serbs at the exit towards Banja Luka, Teslic and Skender Vakuf, the roads out of town. No one could enter or leave Kotor Varos without being checked, without their cars being searched. Might have been just an ordinary small car or a truck, a lorry, all the vehicles were being searched. It was done a lot earlier, a long time before the takeover on the 11th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we are looking at the moment at April of 1992 at the time of this meeting, had this -- blockages been set up, barricades?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the period of time I'm talking about, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I think when the investigator came to see you in October 2000, you marked on a map where these various checkpoints were and I wonder if you can have, please, the document which was attachment 3 to your statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour we have the original here which as you'll see is easier to see because it's in colour, whereas the copy we all got is -- if that can be put onto the ELMO? I can't see any markings on it. Your Honour, that's the original colour map but I don't think Mr. Sadikovic's markings are on that but you can see it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a particular part that you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can make the markings now, if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We have actually got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where do we need to zoom in, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the one, sorry, it's here. This is a better one. Sorry. This is the one he actually marked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let him confirm that he is the author of the markings first, because they are marked but not initialed from what I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move up for just a moment? Yes, you will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just confirm, Mr. Sadikovic, that those are your initials at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are three initials there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think one's in -- I think it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, mine is the one in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we now bring the map down again so we can just see where -- where you marked those crosses, sir, are those where the blockages were, as it were, the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe the locations are not specified but it was along these sections of the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you direct the witness to the top, right-hand corner, where there is a capital M, full stop, S, full stop, dash C and further up, where there is Srpska Kontrol Tatcka, which I suppose that is Serb checkpoints, if I translated well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether it's his writing to start with and what does MSC mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: His initials, Your Honour. The C is for the number of the exhibit. It's in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just confirm, Mr. Sadikovic, is that your writing at the top?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: With your initials, MS, and then dash C for the number of the document, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you look at the statement at page 6, you'll see it's referred to there, the second statement, that is, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Those, obviously, nobody expects them to be 100 per cent accurate, but those are roughly where the checkpoints were? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours may that be made, then, P2327?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the discussion was talking about patrols. Were there patrols set up by the police?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The peculiar situation of Kotor Varos near the front in Croatia and the overall security situation, it was in view of these that we still had mixed patrols, patrolling the town and the local communes, the surrounding local communes. That was according to our plan of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, were there any patrols set up which were not ethnically mixed? First of all in Kotor Varos town itself.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were patrols that were ethnically pure, those were Serb patrols. I'll give you two examples that might have resulted in -- that could have resulted in incidents and conflict. It was in a place called Bilice. It was a Croat village, and there was a platoon, a squad, maybe even a platoon, including between 20 and 30 members of the Serbian Territorial Defence. They were armed. And they went about the village provoking the population. Drago Bandalo, a well-respected citizen, who had previously worked abroad in Austria, he could no longer stand by and watch, so he started arguing with them but that -- it never came to anything more. I'll give you another example. Every single evening in the late -- at late hours of the evening, there was a van, a rather large van, that could hold between 10 and 15 police officers, or uniformed persons, almost every night the van made the rounds of certain locations in the town, and in the local communes of the Kotor Varos municipality. The van was carrying Serbs and the commander was Sasa Petrovic who was always in that van and they would make the rounds of certain points in town, and this was also very irritating for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. citizens, the population. However, we always tried to calm the situation down. I used my authority as deputy commander and people respected me. I always told everyone that they had to keep cool and stay calm -- to prevent conflict from breaking out, to prevent armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, can you look, please, at another map of the area, which has already been exhibited, P2120? If we can just put that on the ELMO? If you can just indicate, Bilice, I think we can see. Is that, if we focus on the top, right-hand corner. Yes, just stop there. Roughly how far was that from Kotor Varos town?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Between 2 and a half and 3 kilometres, perhaps 3 and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put that away again now. Were there any actual incidents of violence breaking out before June the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: There were quite a number of incidents, provocations, rather. I'll just give you several examples where people were being fired at, plum in the middle of the town of Kotor Varos. I'll give you an example. I think it was in March, 1992, perhaps April, I'm not sure. A reserve duty police officer, a member of the Serbian TO, came back from the front in Croatia carrying weapons and in a drunken state, or tipsy perhaps, doesn't make a difference really. He fired at an unarmed civilian who was sitting in a garden near one of the cafes in the town, just across the way from Sumaria [phoen]. Another example from the Zanatski Centar, a group of reserve duty officers just when the inspector from Banja Luka had arrived for the Muslims and Croats to sign an oath of loyalty to the MUP of the Republika Srpska we had a meeting at the pensioners' home but there had been an incident caused by soldiers returning from the Croatian front, a group of soldiers, again fired at a Bosniak, Smajlovic, nicknamed Bili, and the third example I can give you is they fired at a car, a taxi, Ahmet Kovacic from Vecici. An honest man, known as an honest and decent man by Croats, Serbs and Muslims alike. So these are the three examples I can give you now but there were many incidents like that. I personally tried to sort things out when these things happened. I went there to try to calm people down. I'm giving you these three situations because I personally took part in those. I was trying to tell everyone to calm down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the loyalty oath. I want to come on to that in a moment. Still on that document, a meeting was going to be arranged with Stojan Zupljanin on the 8th of April. Did you attend that meeting? First of all, was there such a meeting, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no meeting with Stojan Zupljanin, who was my boss at that time, as a result of those incidents, inspector Savo Todorovic came, who tried to sort the problems out in cooperation with myself and other relevant people in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, let's move to the question of the loyalty oath. At what stage did you, the police in Kotor Varos, get informed about the new loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, just like all the other police stations, the security services centre in Banja Luka, they came to us in Kotor Varos that day and told us that we should take sides, whether we would be part of the Republika Srpska MUP or whether we would remain loyal to the Bosnia and Herzegovina MUP. From what I could tell from the media, and I did have a phone conversation with a colleague of mine from Kljuc, he told me that the Muslims and Croats in Kljuc had been sent off for vacation and that the police station had been taken over by Serbs, of course. In our town it was supposed to be the same day when each and every single individual at the police station in Kotor Varos were supposed to publicly declare their allegiance, but that was the reason why the oath of loyalty was never signed to the MUP of Republika Srpska. I think that was the only police station in the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina where there was no division along these lines and no oath of loyalty to the MUP of Republika Srpska was actually signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, no Serbs or Muslims or Croats in the Kotor Varos police station signed the loyalty oath at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Not officially, we didn't sign any oath. But the Serbs were already working for the MUP of Republika Srpska, they were there when its foundation was proclaimed at the Borac football stadium, they were already working for the MUP of Republika Srpska. They were mopping up the Kupres area and so on and so forth. The Bosniaks and Croats officially did not sign a loyalty oath. Most of them, anyway, I think, would have refused to sign this oath. I'm speaking on behalf of myself, my colleagues, Bosniaks and Croats alike, my commander Nedjo Komavic [phoen] and all the rest. I think only very few Muslims and Croats would have signed, as they did later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you called to a meeting with Stojan Zupljanin around this period of time, May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My chief, my superior, according to our chain of command, informed me that we had a meeting scheduled in Banja Luka with the chief of the public security -- security services centre, Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour this is going to take a little time, perhaps a little time, so perhaps that is an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will break now for 25 minutes starting from now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sadikovic, you were just about to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hold on one moment. We need the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sadikovic, you were about to tell us about this meeting you had with Zupljanin. Your superior, that is Mr. Tepic, had told you to attend this meeting; had he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was the meeting in Banja Luka in the CSB building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did something happen when you arrived at the building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Something did. The colleagues involved in the security of the public security centre were surprised when I came because I was wearing my official cap and the patch, and that is the five-pointed star like everybody else was wearing in Bosnia, and I had all the other insignia and he asked me who was I and whoever saw anyone wearing the -- sporting the five-pointed star still?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, how had the uniform changed, as far as the Serb police were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Instead of the star that we wore and the cap, they started wearing blue berets, and they had the Serb, tri-coloured flag rather than the five-pointed star. And in Cyrillic, they had the flashes on their sleeves, it said, Militia Republika Srpska, Republika Srpska police, and there was nothing in Latin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, at this meeting, what did Zupljanin want?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: That meeting went on for a long time, almost three hours. We talked in a normal atmosphere, and basically, what was said was that I, as a representative of the Bosniak people in the police, and as a senior official, should prevail upon my people and the Croats to hand over their weapons and to sign loyalty to the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, that he wanted me still to be the deputy commander at the police station, that we should maintain the relations in Kotor Varos as such, so that the transition could be done. But basically it was to hand over the weapons and to sign our loyalty to Republika Srpska, that is the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner, just to make this clear for the record, we are talking of Stojan Zupljanin here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And not Slobodan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, Stojan Zupljanin. He was my boss at the time, head of the public security centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you agree to any of those requests or demands, however you put them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it never crossed my mind to do anything like it. I tried to gain some time because I wanted to talk to other people about it, so I asked for about a month to do that, to talk to people, to visit everybody on the ground, to talk to people who could understand. As a matter of fact I was bidding for time so that we could get our bearings and see which way things were developing so that I could seek advice from other people hoping that something else would happen rather than what did happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you give Zupljanin an answer after that month?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Let me tell you, Zupljanin told me that, no, that was much too long, and that there was no way I could get a month, that I could have about seven days, and regardless of my performance and what I thought and regardless of what I did or did not do, they would take over the power in Kotor Varos, as they had planned, as their plans anticipated, envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So he gave you a week. Did you take a week?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Why, of course. Needless to say, seven days, a week, did not mean anything. I needed much more time to see how things would turn there or in Bosnia and all the rest. I couldn't do anything in seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But really what I'm trying to get at is did you ever say to him, no, I won't accept your requests, or demands?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told him openly our meeting, how shall I call it. Well, now suddenly I'm beginning to be afraid. At that time I wasn't afraid and then I told him openly that the weapons would not be handed over because we had all paid for these weapons and the Bosniak and the Croat people had bought every one of these rifles, or other pieces with their own money and therefore those weapons would not be handed over but if they had decided to take over the power, no problem, I and everybody else in the executive government and everything, I will leave and whoever wants to may step in and take over the power but just as long as they let the Muslim and Croat people be. The moment they laid a finger on anyone in our municipality, in our area, then those weapons will be used and we shall come back, but until such a thing happens, no problem, I will leave my duty, I will leave my office and I will sign it because I don't want to have anything to do with that kind of authority, be it I or the majority of people of my origin, and I believe I was speaking in the name of Bosniaks and Croats and that we won't mind the flag or anything, let them take over the power but let them also leave people alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to then look quickly at the events that -- some of the events in the documents that led to the takeover but I want to touch very briefly on a slightly different topic. As a police commander in the SJB in Kotor Varos, from whom did you receive your orders? Or who did the SJB in Kotor Varos receive its orders from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Nedjeljko Maric was the commander, a Croat. Of course, and my colleague, that is a friend, who studied in Sarajevo. We both studied in Sarajevo, and we were on very good terms, personal and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, it's my fault again. It wasn't a proper question. In the chain of command, from whom did the SJB in Kotor Varos take its instructions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: The police station in Kotor Varos received its instructions from the public security centre in Banja Luka. That was the chain of command and communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did the municipal assembly have any authority to issue instructions to the police?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Under normal circumstances, that is in peace time, the interior affairs law, because we have one such, the municipal assembly could propose certain amendments or perhaps if problems arose, if things happened, then they could submit their own proposals, suggestions, and help us to overcome such problems in peace time. But in wartime, under emergency conditions, of course, the competences, the terms of reference of the assembly are different than in peace time so that we were present at meetings when relevant problems were discussed and cooperated and solved all the problems jointly and we always heeded proposals and suggestions that the assembly had to make, all people employed in the municipal hall in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say in wartime, in emergency conditions, it was different. What happened in respect when the assembly could not sit and its functions were performed by a Crisis Staff? Could it, the Crisis Staff, issue directions to the police?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In such instances, of course, the municipal assembly ceased to function, the Crisis Staff assumes all its duties, and the Crisis Staff has more jurisdiction, more competences, over other bodies, that is, and it can have its say in army or police matters too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the chief of police a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ex officio, his office makes him automatically a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Kotor Varos and all the other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I now want just to follow some of the events through the documents until the takeover. Could you be shown, please, Exhibit P2149? This is a report signed by someone who appears to have been a police operative of sorts, in which he talks about the security situation in the Vrbanjci village, where he says that individuals of Muslim background, armed and dressed in camouflage uniforms, have been seen gathering in houses, 60 of these armed individuals, members of the Green Berets, they increase activity when they patrol the village, that it's spreading anxiety and fear amongst citizens of Serbian ethnicity, and because of this, a large number of able-bodied Serbian citizens have come to Maslovare to seek help in the form of protection and weapons so as to be able to put up an adequate resistance to the extremist citizens and the fact that yesterday, and this is dated the 19th of May, at around 2330 hours, armed clashes broke out between Muslim extremists and citizens of Serbian background in the village of Sakan. No one was injured and then it goes on to say that women and children of Vrbanjci and surrounding villages have moved to nearby Serbian villages. And it's a request to arm the able-bodied inhabitants of Vrbanjci. And there is a proposal for an use of a special unit. First of all, do you know anything about these incidents that are being described apparently in these -- in this report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: I can claim under full responsibility that these incidents did not take place, because as a deputy commander, I would have known about it, since I was informed and participated in the solution of all the incidents that had been happening until then, that is gunfire and all the rest, and just as I was informed about them I would have been informed about this and I once again say under full responsibility that these things did not take place except for the patrols and the guards around villages and neighbourhood communities, but without any uniforms, in civilian clothes, there was not a single formation which could get through or be armed and behave in that way. It would have been recorded somewhere in the media or somewhere because that would have been an event which would have necessitated solution and tackling but no such things, rapes or such problems simply did not happen, and all those burials and everything else, now I'm repeating, under full responsibility, that it did not happen because the public would have known about it and we in the police too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. They propose the so-called special unit from Banja Luka come down to Kotor Varos. Were you aware of this so-called special unit?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: I was, yes. Every public security centre has its special unit. We in Kotor Varos had such a unit which was called a manoeuvreing unit and at the level of the public security station, there is a special unit bringing together police members from all the municipalities and that unit is naturally used when there is a serious disruption of public law and order, or some other excesses, when they happened, some major conflicts or wars, on such occasions, in such instances, the heads of public security centres are authorised to use such units but such units never came to Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I'm going to ask you about that document. There is a --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is another document dated the next day but -- which is 2150 but it refers to the same thing effectively. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you look, please, at Exhibit P12 -- sorry, can I just check?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honours but may I add something to what I just said, all the excesses which happened in the municipality of Kotor Varos were recorded and discussed by the municipal assembly, so that this incident would have been recorded and put on the agenda and discussed like all the other problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can you look, please, as Exhibit P1250? This is another one of these reports dated the 8th of June, which refers to Kotor Varos at the end of the first paragraph. For now, Kotor Varos and Banja Luka are the only areas where there has been no operation to return weapons or mop up the ground of Green Berets and HOS members. Now, had you been made aware, Mr. Sadikovic, of the call or the order to disarm that had been issued by the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that. And I claim under full responsibility that the municipality of Kotor Varos, there were no members of HOS or the Green Berets. It was simply used by Serbs where Bosniaks lived, the Serbs said that there were Green Berets and where Croats lived, they said that they had HOS there. But I am saying that there was not a single formation, either belonging to the Green Berets or the HOS before or in the course of the aggression. Later on, there was the self-organisation and all the rest but no formations, there has never been HOS, there's never been any Green Berets. There was only the Territorial Defence of Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then we see the recommendation, we possess firm evidence that there are Green Beret units in the area of Vrbanja, Kotor Varos municipality. I'm not sure where that is. Whereabouts is that, sir? Or is that meant to be Vrbanjci?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Vrbanjci is about 7 kilometres from Kotor Varos, from the centre, if you take the main road, Banja Luka-Kotor Varos-Teslic-Doboj. It's about 7 kilometres away. It's a large neighbourhood community which was economically quite well-standing because a large number of people were migrant workers abroad and because of the Serb propaganda they frequently brought up Vrbanjci and even if their written propaganda, they were saying that a Muslim and Croat police stations would be set up, that some authorities would be set up and so on and so forth but this never happened. It was simply propaganda because it was an economically strong area and there was a rather large concentration of Muslim and Croats and they were afraid of that area and that is why they mentioned the area frequently in their propaganda, however offering no proof of what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I think it's because of the way it's been translated. If one looks at it, it's clearly Vrbanjci, if one looks at the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "We recommend urgent action against these areas for the purpose of returning weapons and getting rid of extremists." That's dated the 8th of June. If you please now look at P234, which is the next day, by the same operative. P234, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's comment in the previous document, it should not be "we recommend." The original says: "We suggest."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 9th of June, Milos: "Following our proposal and the proposals of others, the SDS is due to start an operation soon with the aim of taking over power in Kotor Varos and settling the ethnic tensions in the Kotor Varos SJB and other organs. While this operation is going on, individuals who are in possession of unlicensed arms or those they have obtained from the HDZ or the SDA should be handing these arms in. This operation should be carried out in a synchronised manner with the help of the Banja Luka CSB." Now, had you, as a member of the SDA and a police officer, supplied arms to other Bosniaks in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SADIKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, and I apologise for forgetting to address you as Your Honours, I forgot my manners so please receive my apologies for it. It is not that I do not respect you, I really respect you, and very much, because you are doing a great deal, but I am saying, Your Honours, that I, as a policeman or as a man outside of working hours, I never distributed any weapons because I didn't have them. There were not only Serbs but Muslims and Croats, that is those who were on the reserve force were issued with such weapons but when -- there's exactly -- there was a list of fellows and it wasn't me who distributed them. There was the order from -- which came from Sarajevo, to arm the reserve -- members of the reserve police force so that they were issued with weapons officially. Just as the regulations said it should be done. So I didn't distribute any personal weapons, the -- I didn't distribute any SDA weapons, and I don't think, well I cannot really claim it under full responsibility, but I don't think the HDZ did either. It was people themselves, because they saw what had happened in Croatia and the number of people working abroad, they realised it and they were buying weapons, paying for them with their own money and they were also buying in Croatia on their way back in a different way so they were also buying from Serbs in Banja Luka directly and other places. The sale of these weapons was organised in open and of course, there were smugglers and war profiteers who were obtaining those weapons, selling them and reselling them. It wasn't easy to come by a weapon, I have to tell you in Kotor Varos, or somebody else, you couldn't do it, especially not in any adequate quantities. Perhaps you can smuggle in a rifle or two in your car but to come by any major weapons there was no way you could get into Kotor Varos bringing those because there were controls and checkpoints. Now, individual arming of course there were people who were involved in contraband, that they would bring in 2 -- 1, 2, 3 pieces, smuggling them in and then selling them but nobody distributed any weapons, I did not do it and I don't think that the HDZ did it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was had he or anybody else supplied arms. I think the answer was no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are going to be here for days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In actual fact I know exactly how you feel about it. I felt the same until I realised basically that he was answering the next and the next question. So that's why I kept him going.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. I would have asked the next questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is obvious. On the other hand, please, Witness, slow down because I can notice that you are making it a little bit difficult for the interpreters to catch up with the speed at which you're talking. So please slow down a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, that's all I want on that document. Can you now be shown briefly P959? This is a document from the 1st Krajina Corps and it's dated -- well it was the 8th of June and then somebody seems to have added by hand, the 10th of June. In item 3, paragraph 3, situation on the ground, there is intensive reconnaissance activity and attempts at organising an uprising of the Muslim population outside the conflict areas, particularly in Gradiska and Kotor Varos. Now, was there any attempt to your knowledge to organise a full-scale, armed uprising of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are talking of the 10th of June or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no. I would have known about such organisation, right up until the 11th of June, there was nothing. We stayed there and I was performing my duties normally.
